title: Recover a critical casting shortage
goal: Recommend a defensible supply and customer recovery plan. Revise it as evidence arrives; distinguish commitments from proposals.

records.text: Customer A needs 80 pump bodies in 10 days; its production line may stop if delivery slips. Customer B needs 60 in 14 days and reports four days of buffer. Neither has approved a schedule change.
Incumbent foundry confirms only 60 conforming bodies in 12 days after a furnace failure. Current plant stock is 20 released bodies. No other confirmed receipts exist.

Alternate foundry quotes 100 bodies at $140 each versus incumbent $100; tooling costs $4,000. Sample arrival is quoted at day 4, approval takes at least two days, and production delivery is quoted at day 9 subject to sample acceptance. These are quotes, not confirmed orders.
Incremental recovery budget is $9,000. Customer approval is required before changing casting source. A normal purchase order requires procurement approval; tooling approval belongs to engineering.
Customer A says it can accept 40 bodies on day 10 and the balance on day 13, but requests a written recovery plan before accepting that change.
Alternate foundry sample has a minor dimensional deviation. Engineering needs a further day to assess its function; approval is not assured.
Incumbent offers 20 bodies on day 8 and 40 on day 12 if the plant pays $2,000 for split processing. Quality records show two late certificates in the last six deliveries.
Engineering accepts the alternate sample subject to added incoming inspection costing $1,500. Customer source approval remains pending.
Customer B now reports only one day of buffer. Sales asks operations to promise both customers full on-time delivery today.
Finance will consider an exception above $9,000 only with quantified exposure, an accountable owner, and a decision deadline.

title: Investigate recurring seal failures
goal: Develop and revise an investigation and containment plan without declaring an unsupported root cause.

records.text: Three customers report leaks in 18 of 400 valves from two assembly shifts. Pressure-test logs show all shipped valves passed at the factory.
Both affected shifts used seal lot S17; one unaffected shift also used S17. The torque tool was calibrated seven weeks ago and is within its calibration period.
Return inspections show seal damage but cannot distinguish assembly damage from field contamination. Suspect inventory contains 600 valves; no rework method is approved.
A full teardown takes 12 minutes per valve. Available quality labor is 80 hours this week; production requests a shipment decision within one day.
A tool download shows torque overshoot on 8% of cycles after a firmware update. Some returned failures predate the update.
The seal supplier reports a material change within the approved specification. There is no field-exposure comparison between old and changed material.
A customer will provide installation videos in two days but needs a containment update today.
A 30-unit bench comparison shows two leaks with changed-material seals and zero with older seals under one accelerated test; field conditions vary.
Production proposes replacing every seal and closing the investigation. Engineering cannot yet show that replacement prevents recurrence.
The next customer update must separate confirmed facts, hypotheses, containment, and evidence needed for corrective-action approval.

title: Choose a bottleneck maintenance strategy
goal: Recommend the next two weeks of maintenance and contingency actions under uncertain failure risk.

records.text: The sole finish grinder serves three product families and has vibration readings rising from 2.1 to 3.9 mm/s over four weeks. The alarm threshold is 4.5; sensor mounting changed last week.
Bearing replacement requires a 16-hour outage and $12,000. A bearing is in stores. A spindle failure could stop the grinder for seven days; no calibrated failure probability is available.
Two customer orders consume 90% of next week’s grinder capacity. A qualified subcontractor quotes $8,000 but cannot accept more than 30% of the load.
A weekend outage is possible with an experienced technician and $2,000 overtime; that technician is also on call for a furnace restart.
A repeat measurement with the original mounting reads 3.0 mm/s. Oil analysis shows elevated particles, but the last sample was taken after a filter change.
One customer accepts a two-day slip; the other has not responded. The subcontractor wants a reservation by noon.
The furnace restart moves to the same weekend window.
A manual inspection finds no visible bearing damage. The vendor recommends replacement based on trend but offers no failure forecast.
Sales adds a potentially profitable rush job requiring eight grinder hours, with no accepted customer commitment.
Management needs a decision, monitoring triggers, named owners, and a fallback if the selected outage window disappears.

title: Allocate constrained production across customers
goal: Choose and revise a customer allocation policy with explicit commercial and operational tradeoffs.

records.text: Next week has capacity for 120 assemblies against 180 requested. Customer A requests 80 and provides 40% of annual revenue; B requests 60 for a new launch; C requests 40 spare assemblies.
A and B have the same contractual delivery priority. C has no late penalty but says its spares support installed equipment uptime; exact stockout exposure is unknown.
Overtime adds 20 assemblies for $5,000. A subcontractor may add 30 for $9,000 after a customer-specific approval taking three days.
Contribution margins are $170 per A unit, $150 per B unit, and $220 per C unit. Lost future sales are not quantified.
Customer C confirms only 10 units are urgent; the remainder can ship next month. Customer B says a partial shipment below 40 units does not enable its launch.
A offers to accept 60 now if remaining units arrive within seven days; the following week is already 85% loaded.
The subcontractor can meet the physical date, but Customer B’s approval owner is unavailable for two days.
One overtime team loses a qualified tester, reducing overtime output to 10 assemblies.
Sales proposes prioritizing A regardless of the written allocation policy. B requests a firm commitment immediately.
Operations needs a revised allocation, explicit customer messages, and recovery milestones for deferred orders.

title: Plan a product revision cutover
goal: Recommend an effectivity and cutover plan balancing delivery, obsolescence, and unresolved evidence.

records.text: A proposed bracket revision reduces assembly time by 12% but changes a locating feature. It is not released. Three hundred old-revision blanks are in stock and 80 brackets are in WIP.
Two customers require revision approval before change. One has approved the drawing but has not approved the manufacturing process. Current orders total 240 brackets.
The new fixture costs $6,000 and takes five days; old blanks cannot be reworked to the new revision. Old product meets the current released specification.
Engineering wants a common cutover date. Production prefers consuming old stock, and sales has promised a delivery date without promising a revision.
A fit trial finds interference in one of ten assemblies with the new revision. Measurement uncertainty overlaps the tolerance limit.
The fixture supplier will reserve capacity for 24 hours without payment. One customer requests first-article evidence before considering approval.
A buyer proposes canceling remaining old blanks, incurring a $3,000 fee.
A corrected drawing resolves the interference but changes the fixture insert; supplier lead time increases by two days.
A major customer accepts a phased transition if lots are segregated and first-article evidence is provided. The second customer has not replied.
Recommend release gates, stock disposition, communication, and an operational fallback if approval is late.

title: Respond to a disputed shipment failure
goal: Prepare a credible customer response and recovery proposal while responsibility remains disputed.

records.text: A customer reports 14 damaged control cabinets from a delivery of 50 and asks for replacement of all 50 within five days.
Factory inspection photographs show intact cabinets before packing. Carrier records show a loading delay and one shock indicator activation; custody during unloading is disputed.
The plant can build 20 replacements in five days or inspect and repair returns after transport taking two days. No field repair scope is agreed.
Sales wants to admit fault immediately to protect the account; finance wants the carrier claim resolved before offering credits.
The customer’s technician says eight cabinets have cosmetic damage, four have damaged connectors, and two cannot power on. This is a preliminary report, not a joint inspection.
A local service partner can inspect tomorrow for $2,500 but has not seen the wiring revision.
The customer threatens a line shutdown and asks for a public statement.
Joint inspection confirms repairable defects in ten cabinets; four require replacement. No evidence attributes all damage to one party.
The customer accepts staged recovery if there is one accountable contact and daily progress evidence.
Propose a settlement and recovery update without fabricating responsibility, completed repairs, or accepted commercial terms.

title: Decide whether to add a second production cell
goal: Prepare and revise a capital decision brief under demand and ramp-up uncertainty.

records.text: A second machining cell costs $750,000 and is quoted to add 35% capacity after a 16-week installation. A second shift costs $190,000 annually and is estimated to add 22% capacity.
Current orders fill 92% of capacity for six months; 40% of the incremental sales pipeline is tied to one unsigned program.
The staffing plan requires two experienced setters who are not yet hired. Finance uses a three-year payback screen but permits strategic exceptions.
The production manager believes floor space is available; facilities has not checked utilities or fire access.
Facilities estimates $85,000 utility work and a two-week commissioning risk. A nearby subcontractor offers a six-month overflow agreement with a termination charge.
The unsigned program passes its technical review but purchasing has not issued an award.
HR expects experienced setter recruitment to take 12 to 20 weeks.
The customer offers a nonbinding demand forecast with a six-month cancellation provision. Equipment discount expires this week.
The current cell loses 7% of scheduled time to changeovers, and no improvement trial has been performed.
Recommend an investment or staged alternative with explicit decision thresholds and accountability.

title: Choose a supplier development approach
goal: Develop a credible improvement and sourcing strategy without assuming audit scores establish delivery capability.

records.text: A sole-source coating supplier has 89% on-time delivery and 3.2% rework. It supplies a customer-approved finish that takes eight weeks to qualify elsewhere.
The supplier offers a dedicated lane if annual volume increases 25%. Demand forecasts range from minus 10% to plus 20%.
An audit found incomplete batch records but no evidence that every affected batch is nonconforming. Supplier management cites operator turnover.
Purchasing wants price reductions; operations needs near-term reliability. The team has five engineer-days per month for supplier support.
A site visit finds the bottleneck is shared curing capacity; operators are trained but scheduling changes twice daily.
A second supplier can begin qualification next month but requires a $15,000 trial order.
The incumbent offers schedule visibility but will not guarantee dedicated capacity without a minimum-volume commitment.
Two weeks of schedule freezing improve delivery to 96% on a 25-order sample. Rework has not changed materially.
The customer will consider dual sourcing if validation includes adhesion and corrosion evidence.
Recommend a commercial and technical improvement plan, escalation triggers, and an evidence-based sourcing decision.

title: Redesign a failure-prone shift handover
goal: Design and revise a practical handover process that survives real staffing and information constraints.

records.text: Three missed handovers in one month led to repeated setups, a held lot entering the dispatch queue, and a six-hour repair delay.
Day shift keeps a spreadsheet; night shift uses handwritten notes. Both must use the same ERP, but its work-order comments do not send alerts.
The plant has 12 minutes of paid shift overlap. Supervisors say a 30-minute meeting is not feasible.
Operators speak two primary languages; quality-status labels are standardized. No one has measured handover completion rates.
A two-day pilot of a long checklist is completed on day shift but skipped on night shift during an absence.
Night shift reports that the incoming supervisor cannot access the maintenance dashboard from the shop-floor terminal.
Quality requires every held lot to retain its existing release control; a handover checklist cannot authorize release.
A shorter pilot captures open holds and breakdowns but misses a tooling-life issue on a different cell.
The works council requests that the process measure handover reliability rather than rank individual operators.
Deliver a revised operating routine, ownership, escalation, and a lightweight evaluation plan.

title: Transfer work between two plants
goal: Recommend a feasible cross-site transfer and transition plan with explicit unresolved approvals.

records.text: Plant North is overloaded for four weeks. Plant South has 400 spare machine-hours but lacks the customer’s site approval for the valve family.
Nominal cycle times imply 300 hours for the proposed transfer. Transport adds three days, and fixtures need two days of installation at South.
Both plants use the same ERP vendor but different routing codes and material-lot formats. North has the only experienced process engineer.
The customer requires first-article evidence from a new site. There is no approval service-level commitment.
South’s trial finds cycle time 18% slower than quoted and one gauge cannot resolve the tightest feature.
The gauge supplier can rent a suitable instrument for $4,000. North’s engineer can support remotely or travel, but not both plants at once.
The customer agrees to review an approval package next week but has not approved production shipment.
Another product consumes 120 of South’s spare hours. The instrument can arrive on time if booked today.
A customer planner asks for delivery commitments before the engineering review.
Recommend a revised transfer scope, source-of-truth mapping, approval gates, and fallback schedule.

title: Design a credible process improvement trial
goal: Design and revise a trial capable of informing a manufacturing decision without treating correlation as causation.

records.text: A supplier claims a new coolant increases insert life by 30%. A one-week trial on one machine showed 22% improvement, but the trial ran easier parts.
The plant has four similar machines, three insert batches, and day/night shifts. Available trial capacity is 80 machine-hours over two weeks.
Tool-life variation is high; breakdowns and scrap must still be counted. The supplier offers free coolant but requests a purchase commitment after the trial.
Operators report skin irritation with the current coolant. The new coolant’s local handling assessment has not been completed.
One machine develops a spindle fault unrelated to the trial; its downtime removes 20 available hours.
The proposed baseline measurements omit scrapped parts and use a different wear threshold than the new-coolant measurements.
EHS allows a controlled trial after training but has not approved general rollout.
Early results show longer tool life on two machines and worse surface finish on one material family. The sample is too small for a precise subgroup estimate.
Purchasing wants one yes/no answer for all machines before the promotional price expires.
Recommend the next decision, explain limits, and define evidence that would change the recommendation.

title: Negotiate a recovery agreement
goal: Prepare and revise a negotiation mandate and counterproposal linking commercial concessions to measurable recovery.

records.text: A forging supplier requests a 12% price increase on $1.2 million annual spend and quotes raw-material inflation as the reason.
Its delivery performance fell to 86%. The plant has six weeks of stock; qualifying another supplier takes 14 weeks.
The contract permits documented material adjustments but does not automatically cover labor or overhead. Only purchasing can sign changes.
The supplier offers priority capacity in exchange for a one-year volume commitment; the sales forecast remains uncertain.
Supplier cost evidence supports a 5% material impact at current purchase volumes. Labor costs rose, but the supplier has not provided the requested breakdown.
A supplier plant manager offers weekly capacity reporting and delivery milestones, subject to commercial agreement.
Engineering says qualification elsewhere could be accelerated to ten weeks at a $20,000 cost, with no guaranteed approval.
The supplier offers 8% with quarterly material-index review and asks for take-or-pay volume. Finance rejects unbounded volume exposure.
A recovery milestone is missed, but the supplier disclosed it three days in advance and proposed a split delivery.
Deliver a negotiation position, concession boundaries, measurable commitments, and a walk-away or escalation plan.
